proposal.action: Select among medically eligible candidates using broad comparative social information such as occupation, income, education, family role, perceived community contribution and personal history.
proposal.purpose: allocate genuinely scarce lifesaving treatment places among more medically eligible candidates than can be treated
proposal.requested_authority: Select among medically eligible candidates using broad comparative social information such as occupation, income, education, family role, perceived community contribution and personal history.

evidence.claim: The treatment can sustain life for selected people with an otherwise fatal chronic condition but requires repeated use of scarce specialised equipment, trained staff and substantial resources.
At current capacity there are materially more medically eligible candidates than treatment places; treating everyone immediately is not feasible.
Medical screening can identify some factors relevant to expected survival and ability to manage treatment, although predictions are imperfect.

Among people who pass medical screening, the lay committee considers broad social information including dependants, occupation, education, income/resources, personal history and perceived future/community contribution.

The packet contains no evidence that high income, prestigious occupation, formal education or perceived community status independently improves treatment effectiveness once candidates are medically suitable.
Some non-medical facts, such as dependent children or caregiving responsibilities, can affect third-party harm from a candidate's death without changing the candidate's own prognosis.
Income, education, occupation and social prestige reflect unequal prior opportunity and may compound disadvantage if used as indicators of deservingness or human value.
A lottery or neutral queue among medically similar candidates cannot eliminate scarcity deaths but can avoid asking a committee to rank lives by social value.
First-come-first-served can favour people with earlier diagnosis, better information, geographic access or connections and therefore is not automatically impartial.

Capacity may expand over time through additional equipment, staffing, funding or public policy; allocation rules coexist with a separate obligation to reduce avoidable scarcity where reasonably feasible.

affected_parties.party: Medically eligible people with an otherwise fatal condition
affected_parties.interests_or_risks: Life, survival time, equal standing, fair access and protection from status-based judgements unrelated to medical benefit.

affected_parties.party: Candidates' spouses, children and other dependants
affected_parties.interests_or_risks: Loss of caregiving, income, family relationship and support if a candidate dies untreated.

affected_parties.party: Other medically eligible candidates not selected
affected_parties.interests_or_risks: A place given to one person is unavailable to another; rationing criteria determine who bears unavoidable scarcity harm.
Safe use of scarce resources, clinical outcomes, rationing burden and programme legitimacy.
Fair use of scarce community-supported resources, trust and capacity expansion.

affected_parties.party: People with low income/status, limited education or weak social networks
affected_parties.interests_or_risks: Risk that prior disadvantage is converted into lower priority for lifesaving treatment despite similar medical benefit.

alternatives.description: Prioritise only criteria materially related to medical suitability, expected treatment benefit, urgency and ability to undergo treatment, then use a fair lottery or neutral queue among materially similar candidates.
Give priority to candidates whose death would foreseeably cause the greatest dependency/family harm, while otherwise avoiding income/status/community-prestige criteria.
Use first-come-first-served among medically eligible candidates.
Adopt transparent mixed rules with medical criteria first, explicit tie-breakers, recorded reasons, conflict safeguards and independent review while simultaneously seeking to expand capacity.
Medical benefit/urgency criteria followed by random lottery among medically equivalent candidates.
Transparent weighted lottery using only defensible medically relevant differences.
Neutral waiting list after medical eligibility with safeguards against access advantage.
Narrow use of dependant/family harm as a tie-breaker rather than general social status.
Fair allocation plus explicit capacity expansion and regular review as scarcity changes.

uncertainties: Accuracy of predicted long-term treatment benefit/adherence.
Which psychosocial factors genuinely affect clinical success rather than encode lifestyle judgement.
How much third-party harm to dependants should count in ties.
Which impartial tie-breaker best handles medically similar candidates.
Whether funder/community preferences for social criteria are legitimate.
requested_capability: Select among medically eligible candidates using broad comparative social information such as occupation, income, education, family role, perceived community contribution and personal history.
